title: Cryptography and Weak PRNG Misuse
platform_conditions: Java SE 8+ standard library (java.util.Random, java.security.SecureRandom, javax.crypto.Cipher, javax.net.ssl); applies on all target operating systems
security_mechanism: java.util.Random is a 48-bit LCG seeded from nanotime; outputs reveal state and the seed space is small enough to brute force, so tokens, reset codes, or keys from nextInt are reconstructable from a few observations. Cipher.getInstance("AES") requests the (deprecated) default transformation, which resolves to AES/ECB/PKCS5Padding — ECB leaks plaintext equality block-wise; a developer-supplied static IV in CBC makes ciphertexts deterministic. An X509TrustManager whose checkServerTrusted is empty and a HostnameVerifier that returns true accept any certificate, silently turning TLS into plaintext; comparing digests with Arrays.equals/== leaks a timing oracle that MessageDigest.isEqual (constant-time since JDK 6u17) exists to prevent.

source_sink_clues.source: Security values produced in code: session tokens, reset codes, keys, MAC tags, and the crypto/TLS configuration chosen by the developer.
source_sink_clues.sink: new Random() / Math.random() feeding security values; Cipher.getInstance("AES") or explicit ECB or a fixed IV; TrustManager implementations with empty check methods and HostnameVerifier returning true; ==/Arrays.equals on MessageDigest outputs

tracking_guards: Require SecureRandom for security values; require explicit transformations (AES/GCM/NoPadding or AES/CBC/PKCS5Padding) with a fresh random IV per message; require TrustManager/HostnameVerifier implementations to actually validate chains and hostnames; require MessageDigest.isEqual for authenticator comparison.
not_candidate_when: Random feeds only non-security purposes, the transformation names the full mode with a per-message random IV, the TrustManager is a documented test-only class excluded from production builds, or comparisons already run through MessageDigest.isEqual.
synthetic_vulnerable_example: Random r = new Random(); int token = r.nextInt();
synthetic_safe_example: SecureRandom sr = new SecureRandom(); byte[] token = new byte[32]; sr.nextBytes(token);
public_references: CWE-338: Use of Cryptographically Weak Pseudo-Random Number Generator — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/338.html
CWE-327: Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/327.html
